Rules / Modernization

SK1100 The local is a name for the expression on the next line

A local is initialised and the very next statement hands it straight back, so the name stands for an expression that is used once, immediately.

CategoryModernization
Default severitysuggestion
ScopeSemantic
Needs a compilationyes
Runs under --load=looseno
Cached per fileyes
Fixyes, safe
Language version floor—
Since2.0

Why

var result = Compute(); return result; is an extract-variable that was never undone. The name adds a line and says nothing the expression did not, and a reader still has to check that nothing happens between the two lines before they can read them as one. ⚠ The adjacency requirement is the whole safety argument rather than a narrowing of it. Inlining a temporary is normally unsafe because it moves the evaluation point — everything between the declaration and the use would start running before the initializer instead of after it. With nothing in between there is no order to change, so the initializer may have any side effect it likes and the rewrite is still exact. That is what lets this ship as a fix applicable without review, rather than as the "must require a pure initializer" rule the issue proposed. ⚠ Nothing in the .NET SDK reports this shape. IDE0059 is the neighbouring diagnostic and its subject is a value that is overwritten or never read; measured on a net10.0 probe with EnforceCodeStyleInBuild=true and every code-style severity raised, var t = Compute(); return t; drew IDE0008 and nothing else.

Example

Instead of:

var result = Compute(order);
return result;

Write:

return Compute(order);

When it does not fire

The use must be the statement immediately after the declaration, and must be a return or a throw naming the local and nothing else — return result.Value; is a different rewrite and is not reported. ⚠ The declared type is the second hazard and `var` is not the only answer to it. object M() { long v = 1; return v; } boxes a long where return 1; boxes an int: the declaration performed a conversion the return then did not have to, and deleting it moves that conversion silently. So either the declaration is var, in which case the local's type is the initializer's and there is nothing to lose, or the initializer's type is asked for and must equal the declared type exactly. ⚠ The single-use count is taken over the whole member and not the enclosing block, because a local function declared further down is hoisted and may read the local from above its own declaration; a count that stopped at the block would delete a declaration something still needs. using var, await using var, const, ref and scoped locals are excluded outright — each says something about the local beyond its value and none of it survives deletion — as is a declaration with more than one declarator. A comment anywhere in the region the fix rewrites, the declaration's own leading trivia included, withdraws the finding rather than being deleted with the line. Generated code is excluded.
